content: 1. The care of individuals living with HIV requires a comprehensive approach that integrates prevention, diagnosis, and treatment services for related infections such as tuberculosis, sexually transmitted infections (STIs), hepatitis B and C, and cervical cancer. These services should be closely linked or integrated to ensure effective and high-quality care. 2. Tuberculosis (TB) remains a significant co-infection among people living with HIV. Monitoring and reporting frameworks for TB, such as the 2013 revision, provide essential guidance for tracking and managing this dual burden. 3. HIV testing services should follow consolidated guidelines to ensure accurate diagnosis and linkage to care. These guidelines emphasize the importance of early detection and timely initiation of antiretroviral therapy (ART). 4. Studies, such as those by Nakagawa et al., have demonstrated that the timing of HIV diagnosis significantly impacts the projected life expectancy of individuals living with HIV. Early diagnosis and treatment initiation are critical for improving long-term outcomes. 5. Research by Siedner et al. highlights trends in CD4 counts at the time of care presentation and treatment initiation in sub-Saharan Africa from 2002 to 2013. This meta-analysis underscores the need for earlier engagement in care to optimize health outcomes. 6. Linkage to HIV care following inpatient counseling and testing is crucial for improving survival rates, as shown in studies like those by Wanyenze et al. Ensuring continuity of care after diagnosis is a key component of effective HIV management. 7. Assisted partner notification services have been shown to improve HIV test uptake and case finding, as evidenced by Dalal et al. This approach facilitates the identification of undiagnosed cases and enhances prevention efforts. 8. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends HIV self-testing as a strategy to increase access to diagnosis, particularly in underserved populations. Policy briefs provide evidence and considerations for successful implementation. 9. Managing advanced HIV disease and initiating ART rapidly are essential for reducing morbidity and mortality. WHO guidelines provide detailed recommendations for addressing these challenges. 10. Updated WHO recommendations on HIV prevention, infant diagnosis, ART initiation, and monitoring emphasize the importance of integrating these components into comprehensive care programs. 11. The International Epidemiology Databases to Evaluate AIDS (IeDEA) in sub-Saharan Africa have provided valuable insights into HIV treatment outcomes and program effectiveness from 2012 to 2019. 12. Retention in care and mortality rates on ART in sub-Saharan Africa have been analyzed through collaborative studies, such as those by Haas et al., highlighting the importance of sustained treatment adherence. 13. Interruptions in combination ART significantly increase the risk of clinical disease progression to AIDS or death, as demonstrated by Holkmann Olsen et al. Continuous therapy is critical for maintaining health and preventing complications. 14. Maintaining ART reduces the risk of AIDS-defining events in patients with uncontrolled viral replication and severe immunodeficiency, as shown in studies like those by Kousignian et al. 15. The revolving door phenomenon in HIV care, characterized by patients cycling in and out of care, necessitates a revised service delivery cascade to achieve UNAIDS 95-95-95 goals, as discussed by Ehrenkranz et al. 16. The burden of advanced HIV disease persists despite increasing ART coverage, as evidenced by Osler et al. This highlights the need for targeted interventions to address gaps in care. 17. WHO guidelines on tuberculosis emphasize the importance of collaborative TB/HIV activities to improve outcomes for individuals co-infected with these diseases. 18. Surveillance of antiretroviral drug toxicity and resistance is essential for optimizing HIV treatment programs. Technical briefs provide guidance on monitoring these aspects effectively. 19. Transitioning to new antiretroviral drugs in HIV programs requires careful clinical and programmatic considerations to ensure successful implementation and patient outcomes. 20. The Global Action Plan on HIV Drug Resistance (2017-2021) outlines strategies to address the growing challenge of drug resistance in HIV treatment. 21. Eliminating mother-to-child transmission of HIV and syphilis is a global priority. WHO provides guidance on criteria and processes for validation of elimination efforts. 22. Prevention of mother-to-child transmission of hepatitis B virus through antiviral prophylaxis during pregnancy is recommended to reduce the burden of this infection. 23. Ending inequalities and achieving the goal of ending AIDS by 2030 requires a focus on commitments and targets outlined in the United Nations General Assembly’s Political Declaration on HIV and AIDS. 24. Monitoring and evaluation frameworks for ART in pregnant and breastfeeding women living with HIV, as well as their infants, are critical for ensuring effective care and prevention of transmission. 25. Person-centered HIV patient monitoring and case surveillance systems should integrate data on STIs, hepatitis, and cervical cancer to improve service delivery and health outcomes. 26. WHO’s policy on collaborative TB/HIV activities provides guidelines for national programs and stakeholders to address the dual burden of these diseases effectively. 27. Surveillance of HIV drug resistance in populations initiating ART is essential for guiding treatment strategies and improving program outcomes. 28. Data quality assessment methods for public health information systems are critical for ensuring accurate and reliable data to inform decision-making. 29. Improving data quality in developing countries requires targeted strategies and tools to strengthen health information systems. 30. Viral load testing and HIV patient monitoring systems should be assessed and strengthened to ensure high-quality care and accurate data collection. 31. The Naomi modeling tool provides district-level estimates of HIV epidemic indicators in sub-Saharan Africa, supporting targeted interventions and resource allocation. 32. Promoting the use of routine data throughout health systems is essential for driving decision-making and improving program effectiveness. 33. Integrating related infections into HIV surveillance systems enhances the ability to monitor and address co-infections such as TB, STIs, hepatitis, and cervical cancer. 34. Women living with HIV have a significantly higher risk of cervical cancer, emphasizing the need for integrated screening and treatment services as part of standard HIV care. 35. WHO’s 2022 consolidated HIV strategic information guidelines aim to strengthen programs by integrating data on STIs, hepatitis, and cervical cancer with person-centered HIV surveillance systems. 36. A minimum dataset for monitoring STIs, hepatitis, and cervical cancer in HIV programs includes robust unique identifiers and event dates to link patient experiences across infections and care settings. 37. Comprehensive surveillance systems provide granular information at facility, subnational, and national levels to prioritize prevention and treatment interventions effectively.
